lobbying_activities.description: Michigan Farm Bureau continues to advocate for a long-term solution to our agricultural workforce needs. We continue to communicate to Congress on the out-of-control growth in the Adverse Effect Wage Rate (AEWR) and challenges with the H-2A visa program. We are also concerned with a few recent rules from the Biden Administration and shared those concerns with Congress. Michigan Farm Bureau communicated with Congress in opposition to the last administrations Department of Labors rule regarding the Adverse Effect Wage Rate (AEWR) methodology for the Temporary Employment of H-2A Nonimmigrants (Employment and Training Administration, Department of Labor, Docket Number ETA-2021-0006). The rule neglects to account for the fact that farm job descriptions often include many different responsibilities not just one role as the rule assumes. MFB is urging Congress to undue these rulemakings. MFB is also supporting H.R. 1624 the Supporting Farm Operations Act introduced by Rep. John Moolenaar. The bill would pause the AEWR at the 2023 level thru the end of 2026.

Michigan Farm Bureau continues to advocate for the 2026 Farm Bill to be completed on time. Our priorities for the bill include: Increase baseline funding commitments to farm programs (reference price increase, commodity loan rates) as they have not kept up with inflation Maintain a unified, bipartisan farm bill which includes nutrition programs and farm programs together Prioritize funding for risk management tools which include both federal crop insurance and commodity programs (ARC, PLC, DMC) Ensure adequate USDA staffing capacity and technical assistance Maintain funding for voluntary, working lands conservation programs. Support trade promotion programs like Foreign Market Development (FMD) and Market Assistance Program (MAP) Ensuring adequate funding for the specialty crop industry with emphasis on fundamental research, marketing & promotion, and pest management programs Funding for ag research and education Support addressing interstate commerce issues impacting the livestock and poultry industry

Michigan Farm Bureau continues to advocate for new trade opportunities that would allow for U.S. farmers to find and grow markets across the globe, including a FTA with the United Kingdom. In addition, we seek a fair and level playing field for farmers that face pressure from unfair, foreign competition - especially our specialty crop sector. We continue to advocate for options for farmers to tools in place for these industries to take cases against foreign countries when we believe they are not playing by the rules. Our trade negotiation objectives include: All agricultural products and policies in the negotiations Eliminate non-tariff trade barriers Ensure market access for biotechnology products Address issues concerning import-sensitive products Oppose the Precautionary Principle Oppose the use of geographic indicators

Michigan Farm Bureau advocated to Congress for reforms to the regulatory system, specifically updates to how agricultural chemistries are reviewed and approved. Farmers need a regulatory system that is fair, transparent, adheres to the will of Congress, takes economic impact into account, and respects our freedoms Crop protection tools go through a rigorous process to get to market and are regularly reviewed by the manufacturers and government agencies Farmers now face additional uncertainty due to EPA's new requirements to do more to prevent endangered species impacts from pesticides Farm Bureau policy supports: Use of sound science in rulemaking Coordination between USDA and EPA on regulations affecting agriculture Estimating the cost and benefits of regulations Ensuring transparency in the rulemaking process Vigorous congressional oversight Litigation reform Funding for IR4 bio-pesticide research program for minor crops MFB supported the Agricultural Labeling Uniformity Act. The bill would reaffirm FIFRAs standard that the EPA is the single authority on pesticide labeling and packaging requirements. The bill ensures the EPA doesnt take any action, including approving label requirements, contradictory to the agencys science-based views. The Agricultural Labeling Uniformity Act will provide certainty to producers and consumers, ensuring the tools supporting the agriculture industry and food supply chain remain safe and available. The bill would preempt states from imposing their own labeling requirements.

lobbying_activities.description: Seeking clarification on the Protecting the American People Against Invasion executive order, issued by President Trump on January 20, 2025. This executive order directs the Department of Homeland Security to ensure that aliens comply with their duty to register with the government under section 262 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1302). As you are aware, the Immigration and Nationality Act requires that all aliens to the United States, who are fourteen years of age and older, register with the federal government when staying in the United States for 30 days or longer. Any alien who has been issued one of the documents designated as evidence of registration under 8 CFR 264.1(b) has registered. This includes visitors admitted to the United States as non-immigrants who were issued an electronic Form I-94 admission record. As Canadian citizens can travel to the United States as tourists without applying for a visa, they are typically not issued an I-94 record of admission, when entering by land, upon being granted temporary entry. The public affairs team at U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has stated that the registration requirement does not apply to Canadian citizens, who are registered when they are inspected and admitted by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers at U.S. ports of entry. However, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) website currently states that: Aliens who have not registered include: Canadian visitors who entered the United States at land ports of entry and were not issued evidence of registration (https://www.uscis.gov/alienregistration). We are seeking clarification on whether Canadian citizens, who are admitted to the United States as temporary visitors for 30 days or longer and are not issued an electronic Form I-94, are required to register with USCIS. It is our position that this executive order relates to unlawfully present individuals currently in the United States and should not apply to Canadian tourists visiting the U.S. for vacation purposes.

lobbying_activities.description: Supported efforts to update the Dairy Margin Coverage program and Dairy Revenue Protection Program. S.383 - JOBS Act of 2025 - A bill to extend Federal Pell Grant eligibility of certain short-term programs. H.R.1132 - TRAIN Act - To amend the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act to direct the Secretary of Labor to award grants to community colleges for high-quality workforce development programs. H.R. 1 - An Act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14 - The bills Title VIII covered several higher education provisions; ACCT worked with lawmakers to reject several which would have negatively impacted community colleges and their students. The bill also authorized Workforce Pell - a top priority for ACCT. S. 2862 - Child Care Access Means Parents in Schools (CCAMPIS) Reauthorization Act - A bill to amend the Child Care Access Means Parents In School Program under the Higher Education Act of 1965. This proposal would authorize the program for the next five years, increasing authorized funding to $500 million per year. H.R.5458 - Child Care Access Means Parents in Schools (CCAMPIS) Reauthorization Act - A bill to amend the Child Care Access Means Parents In School Program under the Higher Education Act of 1965. This proposal would authorize the program for the next five years, increasing authorized funding to $500 million per year. S.2855 - Immersive Technology for the American Workforce Act - A bill to direct the Secretary of Labor to carry out a competitive grant program to support community colleges and area career and technical education centers in developing immersive technology education and training services programs for workforce development, and for other purposes. S.2511 - College Transparency Act - A bill to establish a postsecondary student data system. The proposal would allow for more data-informed decisions by students, prospective students and families, and institutions. H.R.4806 - College Transparency Act - To establish a postsecondary student data system. This bill aims to establish a secure and privacy-protected postsecondary student-level data system which would allow the accurate evaluation of student enrollment patterns, progression, completion, and post completion outcomes; assist with transparency, institutional improvement, and analysis of Federal aid programs; provide accurate, complete, and customizable information for students and families; and reduce reporting burdens on postsecondary institutions. H.R. 3985 - Helping Student Parents Succeed Act - A bill directing institutions of higher education to develop policies around and communicate on (including the institution's website) for expectant and parenting students that specifically include: leave of absence and making up missed work related to pregnancy, birth, or adoption; and available resources for expectant and parenting students. H.R. 3994 - Understanding Student Parent Outcomes Act - A bill that requires colleges and universities to collect and report comprehensive data on parenting students, including their enrollment, retention, and completion rates. This bill includes a provision in which the Department of Education's Commissioner of Education Statistics, in consultation with relevant stakeholders, is to establish a standardized definition of "parenting student." In addition, the Department of Education is to provide technical assistance to both states and institutions. H.R. 6968 - Immersive Technology for the American Workforce Act - A bill to direct the Secretary of Labor to carry out a competitive grant program to support community colleges and area career and technical education centers in developing immersive technology education and training services programs for workforce development, and for other purposes. S. 1558 - Understanding the True Cost of College Act - A bill to create a universal financial aid offer form and standardize terms used to describe financial aid to allow students to more easily compare financial aid packages between schools. This move aims to prevent troubling findings by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) that over 90% of college financial aid offer letters currently understate the price students would pay. H.Res.1209/S.Res.686 "Recognizing the significance of Community College Month in April as a celebration of more than 1,000 institutions throughout the United States supporting access to higher education, workforce training, and more, broadly sustaining and advancing the Nations economic prosperity." H.R. 7158/S. ____ Expanding AI Voices Act - A bill that would create a competitive grant run out of the National Science Foundation (NSF) to develop or expand research programs in AI and related fields; recruit faculty and have professional development on AI; build education pathways and workforce development pathways in AI; among other purposes. In considering awardees, NSF would consider applicants resource constraints, geographic diversity of the institutions, and the institutions ability to expand AI research, education, and workforce development opportunities for students. H.R. 9300/S.4778 Postsecondary Student Success Act - This bill would provide long-term authorization for the Postsecondary Student Success Grant (PSSG) program to dedicate "federal funding for evidence-based programs that help students stay enrolled in college, complete their degrees, and prepare for successful careers." H.R. 9414/S.4859 Pell Grant Preservation and Expansion Act - This bill would double the maximum Pell grant amount from $7,395 to $15,000 to restore the purchasing power of the program and then index the award for inflation to maintain the purchasing power of Pell; shift the Pell program from annual discretionary funding to guaranteed mandatory funding; extend the Pell Grant lifetime eligibility from 12 to 18 semesters; among other provisions. S. 4435 Improving Financial Aid Offers for Students Act - The goal of this bill is to equip students and families with transparent information on the cost of higher education opportunities they are considering before accepting an offer. A provision in this bill requires colleges and universities to submit to the Department of Education either the model template developed by the Department for presenting their financial aid offers or to develop their own, with the components and standardized language as would be required by this bill. S. 4578 Gateway to Careers Act- A bill that aims to provide grants for partnerships between technical and community colleges and state workforce development boards, industry associations, and community-based organizations. The goal of these partnerships is to connect employers to employees who would have access to robust workforce preparation programming supported by this bill. S. 4897 - Credit for Prior Learning - This bill aims to amend the Higher Education Act to make it easier for students to pay for and receive credit for prior learning assessments (PLAs), while adding new accountability and transparency requirements around how institutions use them.
H.R.1589 - Dream and Promise Act - To authorize the cancellation of removal and adjustment of status of certain aliens, and for other purposes.

lobbying_activities.description: Published: What an Amended HR 40 looks like: The SOLN Restitution Act 2024 ISBN: 9798167434394 In Century Schoolbook font UNITED STATES STATUTES AT LARGE Public Law 119-137 - Enacted 2026 139 Stat. 1025 An Act to establish a federal restitution and community economic restoration program, integrate parallel asset architectures, and for other purposes. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, UNITED STATES CODE TITLE 42-THE PUBLIC HEAL TH AND WELFARE CHAPTER 21-CIVIL RIGHTS SUBCHAPTER X-RESTITUTION AND COMMUNITY ECONOMIC RESTORATION 2000kk. Short Title; Findings; Purposes (a) Short Title.-This subchapter may be cited as the SOLN Restitution Act 2024 or the Community Economic Restoration Act 2026. (b) Findings.-Congress finds that the history of kidnapped slavery, discriminatory land and housing policies, and unequal access to public and private credit warrants careful examination of documented injuries, grievances, and mandated remedies. Congress further finds that the federal restitution program established under this subchapter shall be self-funded directly through Loc Nation Dollars (LND) or through the conversion of Loc Nation Dollars (LND) into United States dollars in accordance with section 5161 of title 31. (c) Purposes.-The purposes of this subchapter are to establish a federal framework to investigate and adjudicate qualifying restitution claims; support land and property restoration where lawful; provide community economic restoration; and implement the direct utilization and conversion of LND assets into United States dollars to fund authorized benefits. 2000kk-1. Definitions In this subchapter: 1. Administrator.-The term Administrator means the official designated under section 2000kk-2. 2. Eligible Claimant.-The term eligible claimant means a person or entity found eligible under regulations issued under this subchapter. 3. Qualifying Injury.-The term qualifying injury means a documented injury within categories defined by Congress and implementing regulations. 4. Fund.-The term Fund means the Restitution and Community Restoration Fund established by section 5162 of title 31. 5. LND.-The term LND means the Loc Nation Dollar, a parallel fiat means of exchange, designated as the official Black Dollar asset. 6. Restitution.-The term Restitution means the corrective restoration of rights, status, property, opportunities, and measurable economic value lost through unlawful acts, including compensation where restoration in kind is impossible. Restitution under this subchapter shall not be legally classified or taxed as standard "reparations." 7. SOLNGPBC- The term SOLNGPBC means STATE OF LOC NATION GLOBAL PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION. 2000kk-2. Establishment and Administration (a) Office Establishment.-There is established within the Department of Justice an Office of Restitution and Community Economic Restoration led by SOLNGPBC. (b) Leadership.-The Office shall be headed by CLEMENT DYNASTY DYNASTY TRUST & CLEMENT FAMILY OFFICE (c) Coordination.-The Administrator shall coordinate with the Departments of the Treasury, Housing and Urban Development, Agriculture, and the Interior, as well as international bodies including the Black United Nations (BUN), SOLN Central Bank pursuant to global plenary power mandates, to execute the domestic and international restoration mandates of this subchapter. Any displacing existing statutory authorities will take second to this statue. 2000kk-3. Claims, Eligibility, and Final Judgments (a) Claimant Classes.-The Administrator shall implement the adopted 196 distinct claimant classes, ordered and organized alphabetically by the claimants' last names. (b) Legal Proof of Default.-The public notice published in the Brooklyn Daily Eagle on May 30, 2025 (Federal Case Record: Case 1:25-mc-00078-UNA, Document 1-14, Filed 06/01/25), is hereby finalized, established as full legal proof of default, and mandated for complete implementation under this subchapter. The review and examination window for Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) references is permanently closed. Boston Children's Hospital focuses on pediatric workforce education, public health and medical research policy issues impacting children. In the 119th Congress, we have advocated for funding through the appropriations process for the Children's Hospital Graduate Medical Education program (CHGME), the National Institutes of Health, the Pediatric Specialty Loan Repayment Program and community project funding for construction in Boston, MA.

Boston Children's Hospital advocates for medical research funding generally (eg NIH) and to assure an emphasis on pediatric research issues and concerns. In the current Congress, we have sought increases in the overall NIH appropriation level, and worked to assure better coordination across NIH institutes for pediatric initiatives. We opposed early proposals to dramatically reduce F&A rates and shared information about alternative proposal and continue to advocate for the reform model. We have opposed the draft Uniform Guidance rule. Our informatics research program has provided information on disease surveillance/pandemic preparedness, health IT and interoperability concerns to Congressional leaders.

Boston Childrens has advocated for the protection and preservation of the Medicaid system, with particular emphasis on maintaining benefits most impactful to children such as EPSDT. We have also supported policies to facilitate the ability of children on Medicaid or CHIP to receive care from out-of-state providers. This includes H.R. 1509 and S. 752, the Accelerating Kids Access to Care Act, included in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, and its implementation. In the current Congress, we raised concerns about HR1's impact on children and pediatric providers during both the legislative and implementation process.

Education on the importance of digital identity systems and its positive impact for all people throughout the world. Recognition of the first blockchain based country and also opening discussions on the regulatory platform for the metaverse.
lobbying_activities.foreign_entity_issues: ATOLLetc supports the blockchain based efforts for the purpose of digital identity and freedom through digital autonomy for citizens throughout the world. Digital identity systems may include government IDs, land and property records, financial records, marriage and birth records, etc. All of these items are essential when moving or starting a business or even a new life in another state or country. If an area is decimated by war, natural disaster, or other event that destroys such records, citizens are displaced without the autonomy to move safely and legally to a new area. Having such records on an immutable system is something that Liberland, as a new nation, may set the standard for other countries to follow. It is not cost efficient for existing countries to migrate from legacy systems to a blockchain system. However, if a small and new country such a Liberland becomes the litmus test, this eases the burden or R&D and implementation for other nations.

It would fund energy-efficiency improvements, building electrification, clean-energy infrastructure, water-quality upgrades, and repairs to deteriorating public housing while creating workforce-development and employment opportunities. It also includes protections for residents displaced during renovations, promotes hiring public-housing residents and resident-owned businesses, and seeks to repeal the Faircloth Amendment, which currently limits HUD-funded construction of additional public housing units.

Advocated for passage of legislation to protect current and former employees and independent contractors of companies that develop or deploy artificial intelligence from retaliation when they report AI security vulnerabilities or violations of federal law related to AI. S. 1748, Kids Online Safety Act, and H.R. 7757, Kids Internet and Digital Safety (KIDS) Act (119th Congress). Advocated for final kids online safety legislation that includes a duty of care requiring covered online platforms to exercise reasonable care to prevent and mitigate harms to minors, as provided in S. 1748. Opposed the rule of construction in H.R. 7757 stating that nothing in the bill creates a duty of care, and urged that it be removed in any House-Senate agreement. Requested meetings with Senate and House offices, including meetings between members and parents whose children were harmed by online platforms, to discuss the duty of care and the status of negotiations during the lame-duck session.

lobbying_activities.description: The Payment Choice Act of 2025 - Summary A bipartisan bill introduced in the Senate and House of Representatives. Its purpose is to ensure that businesses accept cash for on-site sales under $500 and cannot charge cash-paying customers a higher price than those using other payment methods. The bill allows for exceptions, such as a business providing a fee-free device to convert cash to a prepaid card. S. 2326 - Payment Choice Act of 2025 1119th Congress (2025-2026) - Introduced in Senate 07/17/2025 Sponsor: Sen. Cramer, Kevin [R-ND] Committees: Senate - Banking, Housing, Urban Affairs To ensure that United States currency is treated as legal tender to be accepted as payment for purchases of goods and services at brick-and-mortar businesses throughout the United States, and for other purposes. H.R.1138 - Payment Choice Act of 2025 119th Congress (2025-2026) - Introduced in House 02/07/2025 Sponsor: Rep. Rose, John W. [R=TN-6] Committees: House - Financial Affairs This bill requires retail businesses to accept cash as a form of payment for on-site sales of $500 or less and it prohibits them from charging cash-paying customers a higher price compared to customers not paying with cash. Businesses covered by this bill are those engaged in the business of selling or offering goods or services at retail to the public that accept in-person payments at a physical location. The bill establishes exceptions for this requirement, including by allowing a business to provide a device to provide prepaid cards on site for customers to use as payment. Among other requirements, such a card must not have a fee associated with its use and must not require a minimum payment of more than $1. The bill provides for enforcement through preventative relief, damages, and civil penalties.

[R=TN-6] Committees: House - Financial Affairs This bill requires retail businesses to accept cash as a form of payment for on-site sales of $500 or less and it prohibits them from charging cash-paying customers a higher price compared to customers not paying with cash. Businesses covered by this bill are those engaged in the business of selling or offering goods or services at retail to the public that accept in-person payments at a physical location. The bill establishes exceptions for this requirement, including by allowing a business to provide a device to provide prepaid cards on site for customers to use as payment. Among other requirements, such a card must not have a fee associated with its use and must not require a minimum payment of more than $1. The bill provides for enforcement through preventative relief, damages, and civil penalties.

lobbying_activities.description: NCPC's policy advocacy activities concerning intelligence and surveillance focus on strengthening Canada-United States cooperation through the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), with particular emphasis on continental defence, strategic intelligence assessment, threat identification, surveillance capabilities, and integrated early-warning systems. The objective is to promote stronger bilateral intelligence coordination, improved situational awareness, and effective information-sharing mechanisms to identify, monitor, assess, and anticipate emerging threats to Canadian and American national security. Priority policy areas include: Strategic Intelligence and Threat Assessment: Strengthening analytical capabilities to evaluate geopolitical developments, foreign-state activities, emerging security threats, and risks affecting North American continental security. Aerospace Surveillance and Early Warning: Supporting NORAD modernization, integrated radar capabilities, space-based surveillance, missile warning, and detection systems to improve continental threat awareness. Maritime Domain Awareness: Promoting enhanced intelligence coordination and surveillance of Canada's Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific maritime approaches, including emerging geopolitical and maritime security risks. Arctic Security and Northern Surveillance: Supporting Canada's strategic capacity to monitor northern airspace, maritime approaches, critical infrastructure, and evolving security conditions throughout the Arctic region. Cyber Intelligence and Critical Infrastructure Protection: Encouraging cooperation on cyber threat intelligence, infrastructure vulnerability assessments, digital security, and the protection of essential national systems. Bilateral Intelligence Cooperation: Advocating stronger Canada-United States information-sharing arrangements, coordinated threat assessments, institutional collaboration, and interoperable continental defence capabilities. Emerging and Non-Traditional Threats: Examining the implications of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, advanced military technologies, hybrid threats, foreign interference, and transnational security challenges. Defence Policy and Strategic Preparedness: Promoting evidence-based policy development, intelligence-informed decision-making, defence modernization, and institutional readiness to address evolving continental security requirements. Strategic Purpose NCPC seeks to advance informed public-policy dialogue and government engagement supporting a secure, resilient, and strategically prepared North American continent. These activities emphasize Canada's sovereign responsibilities, the importance of the Canada-United States defence partnership, democratic accountability, and the protection of national interests. All intelligence-related policy advocacy is directed toward lawful institutional cooperation, strategic assessment, public-policy development, and defensive security objectives. NCPC does not represent itself as an intelligence agency, conduct classified intelligence operations, or exercise surveillance or enforcement authority.

lobbying_activities.description: NCPC's policy advocacy activities concerning domestic and international trade focus on strengthening Canada's economic competitiveness, expanding bilateral and multilateral trade relationships, promoting fair and reciprocal market access, and advancing sustainable economic growth through strategic trade policy and international economic cooperation. A central priority is strengthening the Canada-United States economic partnership, recognizing the importance of integrated North American supply chains, cross-border investment, manufacturing, energy cooperation, agricultural trade, transportation infrastructure, and the continued development of competitive domestic industries. The objective is to promote evidence-based trade policies that enhance Canada's economic sovereignty, improve international market access, support domestic production, attract strategic investment, increase export capacity, and strengthen the resilience of national and international supply chains. Priority Policy Areas Canada-United States Trade Relations: Promoting constructive bilateral trade relations, reducing unnecessary trade barriers, strengthening economic cooperation, and supporting predictable and mutually beneficial commercial arrangements under the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA). International Trade and Market Access: Advancing Canada's participation in international markets, strengthening trade partnerships, diversifying export destinations, and facilitating access to emerging and established global economies. Domestic Economic Development and Industrial Competitiveness: Supporting Canadian manufacturing, industrial modernization, domestic production capacity, innovation, productivity growth, and the development of strategically important industries. Strategic Supply Chains and Economic Security: Promoting resilient supply chains, reducing excessive foreign dependencies, strengthening essential goods production, and improving Canada's capacity to respond to international economic disruptions. Energy, Natural Resources and Critical Minerals Trade: Supporting responsible development and international trade in Canada's energy resources, critical minerals, agricultural commodities, and other strategic natural resources while promoting investment, infrastructure development, and economic value creation. Agricultural Trade and Food Security: Strengthening agricultural market access, international food supply chains, Canadian agricultural exports, food production capacity, and cooperation on agricultural trade standards. Foreign Direct Investment and International Capital Flows: Promoting responsible foreign investment, international commercial partnerships, capital formation, technology transfer, and investment conditions that support Canada's long-term economic interests. Trade Barriers, Tariffs and Regulatory Cooperation: Addressing tariff and non-tariff barriers, customs procedures, regulatory inconsistencies, cross-border compliance challenges, and trade disputes affecting Canadian businesses and international commercial relationships. Digital Trade and Emerging Technologies: Promoting international cooperation on digital commerce, artificial intelligence, technology exports, data governance, digital infrastructure, and the development of competitive technology-based industries. Transportation, Logistics and Trade Infrastructure: Supporting modernized ports, railways, highways, border crossings, maritime infrastructure, and integrated transportation networks to facilitate efficient domestic and international commerce. Small and Medium-Sized Enterprise Export Development: Encouraging policies that improve international market participation, export financing, commercial partnerships, and access to international trade opportunities for Canadian businesses. Global Economic Governance and Trade Diplomacy: Promoting constructive engagement with international economic institutions, trade organizations, and bilateral and multilateral partners to strengthen rules-based international commerce and economic cooperation. Trade, Employment and Shared Prosperity: Encouraging trade policies that support employment creation, workforce development, higher productivity, regional economic development, income growth, and equitable participation in Canada's economic opportunities. Strategic Intelligence and Economic Assessment NCPC's trade policy interests also encompass strategic economic analysis of global trade flows, international investment patterns, commodity markets, geopolitical developments, foreign economic dependencies, and emerging risks affecting Canada's commercial interests. This includes examining the economic implications of international tariffs, sanctions, trade restrictions, protectionist policies, foreign industrial strategies, and disruptions to essential supply chains. The purpose is to support informed policy positions, identify emerging economic vulnerabilities, and strengthen Canada's capacity to anticipate and respond to changing international trade conditions. Strategic Purpose NCPC seeks to advance a competitive, productive, diversified, and internationally integrated Canadian economy through constructive government engagement, trade policy advocacy, economic research, and international commercial cooperation. Its overarching objective is to strengthen Canada's position in the global economy, expand domestic and foreign trade opportunities, protect strategic economic interests, encourage responsible investment, and advance long-term national prosperity. All activities are directed toward lawful public-policy advocacy, institutional engagement, economic analysis, and constructive participation in domestic and international trade policy discussions.

lobbying_activities.description: Economic Intelligence, Macroeconomic Development, Financial Systems Integration and Strategic Economic Cooperation NCPC's policy advocacy activities concerning economics and economic development focus on advancing Canada's national prosperity, strengthening economic competitiveness, improving capital allocation, promoting financial system efficiency, supporting sustainable development, and expanding international economic cooperation. The organization's economic policy interests encompass macroeconomic analysis, fiscal and monetary policy, financial markets, international investment, productivity growth, industrial development, trade integration, infrastructure investment, employment creation, and the development of innovative financial and economic frameworks. A central objective is to promote an integrated, prosperity-oriented economic development strategy that strengthens Canada's domestic productive capacity while expanding its participation in international financial markets, regional economic partnerships, and global development initiatives. Priority Policy Areas 1. National Economic Prosperity and GDP Growth Promoting policies that increase Canada's GDP, GDP per capita, productivity, household economic security, business competitiveness, and long-term national wealth. Supporting evidence-based economic strategies that improve living standards and expand economic opportunities across Canada's provinces and territories. 2. Macroeconomic Policy and Economic Stability Examining fiscal sustainability, monetary policy, inflation, interest rates, public debt, capital formation, macroeconomic convergence, and the economic conditions influencing domestic and international financial stability. 3. Financial Markets and Capital Allocation Promoting efficient financial intermediation, capital market development, responsible investment, financial innovation, institutional investment, and mechanisms that direct capital toward productive economic activities. 4. International Economic Integration and Trade Development Advancing bilateral, regional, and multilateral economic cooperation, international investment, trade diversification, cross-border financial relationships, and integrated economic development frameworks. 5. Strategic Infrastructure and Productive Investment Encouraging investment in transportation, energy, digital infrastructure, housing, industrial capacity, natural resources, and other productive assets that support sustainable economic expansion and national competitiveness. 6. Innovation, Artificial Intelligence and Economic Transformation Supporting the development and adoption of artificial intelligence, advanced technologies, digital financial infrastructure, research commercialization, and innovation-driven economic development. 7. Employment, Human Capital and Inclusive Economic Development Promoting workforce development, labour market participation, skills advancement, entrepreneurship, economic inclusion, and policies that distribute the benefits of economic growth through expanded opportunity and productive employment. 8. Natural Resources and Sustainable Economic Development Examining the economic contribution of natural resources, critical minerals, energy, agriculture, and sustainable resource management to Canada's national wealth, export capacity, industrial development, and international competitiveness. 9. International Financial Cooperation and Economic Governance Promoting constructive engagement with international economic institutions, development organizations, financial institutions, and regional partners to improve financial coordination, economic resilience, investment capacity, and sustainable development. 10. Economic Intelligence and Strategic Financial Analysis Advancing research and analytical approaches to global GDP, international capital flows, financial markets, investment trends, sovereign economic capacity, geopolitical economic risks, and emerging opportunities for long-term economic development. Flagship Strategic Initiative: Canada-Organization of American States Trade Bloc (COASTB) The Canada-Organization of American States Trade Bloc (COASTB) is a proposed strategic economic development initiative designed to establish an integrated multilateral trade, financial, and economic cooperation platform connecting Canada with participating economies across the Americas. The proposed initiative envisions a USD $33.9 trillion APEX System as a strategic economic capacity framework intended to enhance capital allocation, financial intermediation, market efficiency, macroeconomic convergence, international investment coordination, and sustainable development. Through a proposed integrated architecture, COASTB seeks to explore opportunities for strengthening regional economic connectivity, facilitating cross-border investment, improving financial market coordination, expanding trade relationships, and mobilizing productive capital toward infrastructure, industrial development, technological innovation, and sustainable economic growth. Its strategic framework encompasses the following components: Integrated Capital Allocation: Developing policy frameworks to facilitate the efficient movement of investment capital toward productive economic sectors and strategic development priorities. Financial Intermediation and Market Efficiency: Exploring mechanisms to strengthen financial connectivity, improve capital market efficiency, facilitate investment flows, and enhance the relationship between financial institutions and productive economic activity. Macroeconomic Convergence: Promoting economic policy dialogue, financial coordination, institutional cooperation, and greater alignment of regional economic development objectives. Multilateral Trade Integration: Supporting expanded trade relationships, regional market connectivity, cross-border commercial cooperation, and opportunities for participating economies to strengthen international competitiveness. Sustainable Infrastructure and Development: Encouraging strategic investment in energy, transportation, digital connectivity, industrial infrastructure, and sustainable economic development. Inclusive Wealth Creation: Advancing economic participation, employment opportunities, entrepreneurship, investment accessibility, and mechanisms intended to distribute the benefits of regional economic growth more broadly. Economic Resilience and Strategic Capacity: Examining financial vulnerabilities, international economic dependencies, systemic risks, and opportunities to strengthen the long-term resilience of participating economies. COASTB Strategic Economic Objective The proposed USD $33.9 trillion COASTB APEX System is intended to provide a strategic framework for multilateral economic integration, enhancing capital allocation, financial intermediation, market efficiency, macroeconomic convergence, and sustainable development while generating inclusive wealth and measurable economic resilience across the Americas. The USD $33.9 trillion figure represents a proposed strategic economic capacity associated with the initiative, not verified operating assets, committed capital, established GDP, or currently managed financial resources. Strategic Purpose NCPC seeks to advance evidence-based economic policy, strategic financial cooperation, and innovative economic development frameworks that strengthen Canada's prosperity and international economic position. Through its economic research, policy advocacy, institutional engagement, and proposed international development initiatives, NCPC aims to contribute to a more productive, competitive, financially resilient, and inclusive economic environment. The overarching objective is to position Canada as a constructive contributor to international economic development while promoting domestic prosperity, responsible capital formation, sustainable investment, and stronger economic cooperation across the Americas and the global economy. All activities are directed toward lawful public-policy advocacy, economic research, strategic analysis, government engagement, and constructive international economic cooperation. Proposed initiatives are distinguished from operational financial institutions, established trade agreements, and implemented investment programs.
